content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) prevention, specifically focusing on TB preventive treatment (TPT). This handbook, published in 2020, provides detailed guidance on implementing and scaling up TPT services globally. It emphasizes the importance of identifying individuals at high risk of developing TB disease, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV), household contacts of TB patients, and individuals with immunodeficiency conditions. These groups are prioritized for TPT to reduce their risk of progressing to active TB disease. The handbook outlines the steps required to implement TPT effectively, including ruling out active TB disease through clinical and radiological assessments, testing for TB infection when necessary, and initiating preventive treatment. The WHO End TB Strategy prioritizes TPT as a critical intervention under its first pillar, aiming to achieve 90% coverage of TPT among PLHIV and household contacts of TB patients by 2025. Despite the gradual expansion of TPT services worldwide, access remains limited, particularly among at-risk populations. For example, in 2018, only 8 million PLHIV, 350,000 children under five years of age, and approximately 80,000 individuals aged five years or older received TPT. This low coverage underscores the urgent need for ministries of health to redesign TPT programs, mobilize resources, and align with the latest WHO guidelines to scale up services rapidly. The handbook also addresses the challenges associated with the cascade of care for TPT, which includes identifying eligible individuals, ensuring they complete medical evaluations, initiating treatment, and supporting adherence to therapy. Significant losses occur at various stages of this cascade, with less than 20% of eligible individuals completing the entire process. Strengthening each element of the cascade is essential to improve TPT coverage and reduce the reservoir of TB infection. To support implementation, the handbook provides tools, job aids, and monitoring indicators tailored to local contexts. It also emphasizes the integration of TPT services with TB case-finding efforts, ensuring that individuals with presumptive TB are tested using rapid molecular diagnostics and treated if necessary. For those without active TB disease, TPT should be initiated to prevent progression to active disease. The WHO operational handbook is intended for policymakers, program managers, healthcare workers, and other stakeholders involved in TB and HIV programs. It serves as a comprehensive guide to scaling up TPT services, with a focus on high TB and HIV burden settings, while also being applicable to low TB burden countries pursuing TB elimination.
